newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: China's Zhu to visit Australia as relations warm.
newsitem.headline: China's Zhu to visit Australia as relations warm.

text.p: Chinese Vice Premier Zhu Rongji will visit Australia this month in a surprise sign of warming ties seen as a reward for Canberra's refusal to join a Western attempt to censure Beijing on human rights.

Zhu, the architect of China's economic reforms and state business restructuring, will arrive on May 23 for week-long talks with government and business leaders, Trade Minister Tim Fischer said in a statement on Tuesday.
He will be the most senior Chinese leader to visit since Prime Minister John Howard's conservative Liberal-National coalition won power in March, 1996.

Zhu, accompanied by a delegation which includes 10 members of at least vice-ministerial rank, will meet Howard, Treasurer Peter Costello, Foreign Minister Alexander Downer, Fischer and other national and state ministers.
He will travel to Canberra and the states of New South Wales, South Australia, Western Australia and Queensland.
The unscheduled visit follows Zhu's cancellation of a planned trip to the Netherlands, Ireland, Austria and Luxembourg in late May.
Beijing-based diplomats have said that visit was cancelled as a mark of anger over a resolution in the United Nations Human Rights Commission to censure China's human rights record.
The diplomats said the move was aimed at the Netherlands, which officially co-sponsored the resolution, although the other three countries had also supported the resolution.

Australia, which had co-sponsored the annual resolution for the past six years, refused to do so this year after Howard persuaded Beijing to establish a formal dialogue on human rights. Australia's decision was strongly criticised by human rights groups.

One Canberra-based China-watcher said Beijing was now rewarding the Howard administration for the move. Sino-Australian relations since Howard's March 1996 election had been sourced by a series of minor spats.
"This is a nice little pay-off," he said.
China is Australia's fifth-largest trading partner, with two-way trade worth A$8 billion (US$6.2 billion) in 1996 and growing at about 20 percent a year.
